title: Let checkout requests wait for the exchange rates

blocks.text: The checkout service converts prices with exchange rates that a loader thread reads from storage once, at startup. Requests arrive from the first second, often before the rates do. A request must then wait for them, but not for ever: after the configured timeout it fails with a `TimeoutException`, and the load balancer retries it on another node. The loader reads into a scratch map, which it clears and reuses once it has handed the rates over.

items: `onLoaded(...)`, called once on the loader's thread;
`awaitLoaded()`, called by every request before it reads the rates.

blocks.text: When you're done, no request answers from rates that aren't fully loaded, a request that comes early waits and then answers, and one that has waited the whole timeout fails with `TimeoutException`. The `rates` field stays a plain field. About five lines in total.
The tests load the rates and make requests on threads of their own, and hold the loader in the middle of its work.

cases.says: once the loader thread has delivered the rates, requests on other threads get the loaded rates
a request does not go on while the loader is still storing the rates; it answers from the stored rates once the loader is done
when the rates don't arrive within the timeout, a request fails with TimeoutException instead of answering from no rates
a request that arrives before the rates waits for them and then answers
the cache keeps answering after the loader clears the map it delivered

origin.section: Only an Acquire That Succeeds, on the Same Object, Gets the Edge

concepts: Only an acquire that succeeds gets the edge: an await that returned false, a get that timed out or returned null, or a poll that returned null orders nothing.

A java.util.concurrent hand-off (submit to task, task to Future.get, countDown to await, put to take, map put to get) is a happens-before edge, so data passed through it needs no volatile fields or locks of its own.
